Studying the history of medieval Britain
Introduction to Making a Living in the Middle Ages: the People of Britain
from the 9th to the 16th century
There are many reasons why we should explore the economic history of medieval Britain.
First of all, economic history is the only branch of history which gives pride of place to the
whole population, because through the study of the economy we can understand the everyday
lives of working people. It is sometimes thought that historical change occurred because
crucial decisions were taken by powerful elites of rulers, aristocrats and merchants. But more
often, change emerged from the combination of thousands of uncoordinated actions,
involving people at all levels. Contrary to what many have imagined, dictatorial decisions
from above were not the motive force behind many economic changes; rather, the opposite
was true. The most important driving force was often competition and frictions between
different groups; not just between lords and peasants, or merchants and artisans, but also
between laymen and clergy, higher aristocrats and gentry, and subjects and the state. In
reality, a society that appears to have been governed by rigid laws and customs actually
allowed people to take initiatives.
Secondly, all other human endeavours depend on the economy, the production of food and
other goods, and this means that any investigation of non-material things must take the
material base into account. Economic history is a unifying subject, not taking us into an
obscure byway of the past, but acting as a crossroads from which we gain access to the
history of the environment, culture, politics and thought.
Economic historians are concerned with two types of change. One focuses on the ups and
downs of economic life, both the short-term fluctuations in prices and trade, and the long-
term movements of growth and decline. The other type is concerned with structural changes,
such as the emergence of towns, or shifts in the distribution of land and the control of farming
between social groups. Both are necessary to look at for a rounded understanding of what
happened.
So why go back to such a remote period as the Middle Ages? The past has always attracted
our curiosity, and there is no reason to think that the period before 1520 offers us any less
interest than the twentieth century or any other period in between. Medieval people were as
lively, active and complicated as those of any other time, and they are as worthy of our
attention as those of later centuries. They pose at least as many dilemmas and puzzles of
interpretation. More particularly, there is a special fascination in revealing the thoughts and
actions of people living in an age so unlike our own, when most people worked on the land,
and were dominated by an aristocracy and a powerful church. The past fascinates us because
it was different, and the Middle Ages were very different.

11
Last, but not least, later periods cannot be fully understood if we do not understand their
predecessors. In Britain, we owe the majority of our towns, villages, boundaries, roads and
institutions to the Middle Ages. The words that we use to describe economic life, such as
farmer, wages, fees, capital and interest, were all used in the Middle Ages. Thus, our world is
based on foundations laid before 1520, and we therefore need to know something about that
phase of our development.
Choosing the dates for the beginning and the end of a historical period always presents
dilemmas. The economic history of Britain in the Middle Ages could be said to have begun
with the large-scale clearances of land for planting in the third millennium BC. Much land
which was under cultivation in 850 AD had been cultivated since prehistoric times. It might
be tempting to start with Roman Britain, the period from the first to the fifth centuries AD,
when cities and lines of communication of lasting importance were established. The
barbarian invasions of the fifth and sixth centuries, when the first English-speaking settlers
landed and embryonic states developed, offer another convenient point to begin.
However, the ninth century has been chosen because it marks the beginning of a great
formative period, when essential elements in the political, social and productive structure
were put into place. The pattern of villages and towns which provided the place of residence
and work for many medieval (and modern) people was established in the period 850-1100.
The basic principles of the social hierarchy, with a dominant aristocracy living on the rents
and services of a subordinate peasantry, and a network of exchange based on towns, all owe
their origins to this period.
Choosing a point at which to end the work poses fewer problems. The two centuries after
1100 can be summed up as a time of expansion, followed by a profound crisis in the
fourteenth century, marked by the Great Famine (1315-1317), when a considerable
proportion of the population died of hunger, and the Black Death (1348-1360), when many
of those who survived the famine met their deaths. However, the story could not end at that
point, because a combination of contraction and new developments flows from the crisis, and
these need to be followed through until the early sixteenth century. A new era began with the
end of a period of low population in 1540, the price inflation which occurs just before 1520,
and the redistribution of property associated with the 1530s; continuing the story until that
point gives a clearer indication of the years to come than would be the case if it stopped in the
mid-fourteenth century.
